audience: General YouTube viewers who have been pitched an MLM by a friend or seen one promoted online; no knowledge of compensation plans, surveys or regulators assumed.
title: How Much Money Do MLM Participants Actually Make?
question: How much money do MLM participants actually make?
alternates: Can You Really Get Rich Recruiting People Into an MLM?
What MLM Income Disclosures Admit in the Fine Print
premise: Four independent documents answer the question the same way, each with a limit the video must state. AARP's 2018 probability sample of 601 participants found 47% lost money and 25% made any profit, self-reported. The FTC's 2024 review of 70 income disclosures found most participants made $1,000 or less a year, before expenses. Taylor's analysis of 30 companies gets to 99.6% losing money only after subtracting required purchases, so that figure depends on his method. The downline promise is structurally true (the pay plans do route income from recruits) and practically false for almost everyone: in rank tables over 90% sit in the lowest cohort averaging under $100. The exhaustion arithmetic is illustrated by Taylor, not tested by any study.
whyWatch: Everyone has been pitched by a friend. The companies' own income disclosures, a nationally representative survey and a 30-company analysis all say the same thing, and the pitch's central promise, leveraged income from a downline, is where the numbers are most revealing.
tension: The pitch sells leverage: recruit and earn from everyone below you. The disclosures show the leverage is real for a fraction of a percent and the structure guarantees most people sit at the bottom.

arc.hook: A friend's message: join under me, build a team, earn while you sleep. How much do people in that position actually make?
arc.conflict: The companies publish income disclosures. Read one aloud: median earnings, share with zero income, and what the fine print says is not deducted.
arc.evidence: AARP's survey (47% lost money), the FTC's 70-disclosure review (most under $1,000 a year before expenses), Taylor's 30-company analysis (99.6% lose after required purchases, by his method), and the rank tables showing where the downline income goes.
arc.resolution: The leverage exists, for the top fraction of a percent, because the plans pay for recruiting rather than retail; most participants are structurally at the bottom.
arc.takeaway: Ask for the income disclosure before joining, read the expense fine print, and treat 'leveraged income' as the company's revenue model rather than yours.

evidence.note: Of the 601 surveyed participants, 25% made any profit over their whole time in the MLM: 14% under $5,000, 6% $5,000 to $9,999, 3% $10,000 to $24,999, 3% $25,000 or more, and 3 people (0.5%) $100,000 or more; 47% lost money (41% under $5,000, 3% $5,000 to $9,999, 1% over $10,000) and 27% broke even; all self-reported.
evidence.why: the survey measures exactly the claim's population and question (profit or loss over the whole time in the MLM, nationally representative sample); self-report limits precision, not scope, and the narration must say so

evidence.note: Most of the 70 disclosures leave people out of the income distribution: 29 exclude everyone who earned no commissions and another 24 exclude participants the company deems inactive, so published figures understate the share with no income.
evidence.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

evidence.note: Across 30 MLMs' own income disclosures, after subtracting required purchases and modest expenses, 99.12%-99.97% of participants (average 99.6%) lost money and about one in 238 profited; Nu Skin's own 2008 report shows 85.89% of active distributors earned no commission at all.
evidence.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

evidence.note: FTC summary of 70 income disclosures: most participants made $1,000 or less a year before expenses, and in at least 17 MLMs most participants made nothing at all.
evidence.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

evidence.note: Nationally representative probability sample of 601 current/former MLM participants: 47% reported losing money, 27% broke even and only 25% made any profit over their whole time in the MLM.
evidence.why: the verdict bears on the claim as worded

evidence.note: Across the 27 MLM disclosures giving the figure, the share of participants with no income exceeded 50% in 17, and staff's calculations show the vast majority received $1,000 or less per year (under $84/month) before expenses.
